Would time work differently in our solar system compared to the rest of outer space

Time is relative. Every point in space experiences time differently, and the only objective way to reason it is using a mathematical spacetime construct.

Black holes can already exist at the same mass as our sun, but at a much smaller radius. We would "experience" time in the same way we do now without noticeably different relativistic effects because we are the same distance away. The general equation for the force due to gravity, F = GMm/r^2, is already often used in a way that assumes the entire mass of a body is located at a point in its center because we normally only care about finding the force outside the planet. That's why it's more complicated to find the gravitational force inside a planet somewhere. (Any point where the radius is less than the radius of the body.)

Basically, assuming we were the same distance away from its center point, and the black hole is the same mass as our current sun, it would be exactly the same as if we were orbiting our regular sun, except slightly colder and darker of course. :^)
